Fun but challenging platforming game to play.

This is an excellent game. While it may seem aimed at younger players due to its visual style, it is actually suitable for players of all ages who enjoy challenging puzzles and exploration. I played it many years ago and got stuck. But after watching my nephew play it on my computer recently, I was drawn to it again and decided to finish it. It's a challenging game. You have to find the right perspective to solve the puzzles and defeat bosses, and you have to retry many times. The control is fluent. Very well-designed control. The map is large. There are many treasure hunts, ability upgrades, secret stages, and a lot of fun. Both music and anime are excellent. It’s Metrovania, but it’s not just Metrovania. Definitely worth playing. I’ve completed it with all achievements unlocked. It took me over 40 hours in total, and I enjoyed every minute in the game.

A história é bem leve, quase um conto de aventura. Você controla o Jin, que acaba sendo amaldiçoado e transformado em diferentes formas de criaturas ao longo da jornada. Não é algo muito profundo, mas funciona bem como motivação pra exploração e progressão.

O gameplay é o ponto mais forte do jogo. Ele mistura plataforma com metroidvania de um jeito muito bem feito. Cada forma que você desbloqueia muda completamente a forma de jogar, seja nadando, quebrando blocos ou voando, e isso abre o mapa de forma bem natural.

A sensação de progressão é muito boa. Você começa limitado e aos poucos vai expandindo suas possibilidades, voltando em áreas antigas com novas habilidades pra acessar segredos e caminhos escondidos.

Os puzzles e desafios de plataforma são bem variados. O jogo sabe equilibrar bem momentos mais tranquilos de exploração com partes mais técnicas que exigem precisão.

A exploração é bem recompensadora. Sempre tem algo escondido, seja upgrade de vida, moedas ou áreas secretas que incentivam você a olhar tudo com atenção.

Visualmente ele é muito bonito. O estilo desenhado à mão é bem vibrante e cheio de personalidade, com animações bem fluidas que dão vida ao mundo.

A trilha sonora ajuda bastante a criar essa atmosfera de aventura leve, sem ser invasiva, mas sempre presente de forma agradável.

O que mais me pegou foi essa sensação de evolução constante. Cada nova transformação muda não só o que você pode fazer, mas também como você pensa o mapa.

É aquele tipo de jogo que parece simples no começo, mas vai se revelando cada vez mais interessante conforme você avança, principalmente pra quem gosta de exploração e progressão bem construída.

● 画面是比较可爱的手绘卡通风格，整体很不错，不过少数地方前景背景区分度不够，略影响体验。
● 在Metroidvania的核心机制下也有自己的特色。变身为各种动物并使用各种独特技能的设定很有意思；虽为2D平台，但远景并不只是背景，人物有时会进入远景中行动，有创意。

[h1]🎮 Reseña de Monster Boy y el Reino Maldito[/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Monster Boy y el Reino Maldito es ese recordatorio incómodo de que los juegos de Acción/Aventura/Indie todavía pueden ser una carta de amor al plataformeo clásico… sin necesidad de venderte un “roadmap” ni una crisis existencial en forma de cinemática de 40 minutos. Aquí vienes a saltar, explorar, pegarle a cosas y desbloquear habilidades como si el metroidvania fuera una religión (y tú, su devoto con mapita en mano).

La propuesta es simple pero adictiva: un mundo interconectado, progresión por transformaciones/habilidades y esa deliciosa sensación de “ahora sí puedo volver y abrir ESA puerta que me vio sufrir hace 3 horas”. La primera impresión es: “Qué bonito, qué fluido… ah, ok, el juego quiere que me pierda a propósito”. Y sí: lo logra.

En resumen: un indie con alma de clásico, presentado con el brillo suficiente como para que te sientas en 1993… pero con comodidades modernas para que no termines escribiendo un manifiesto en el foro.

[h2]Lo Heroico y lo Mald… No Tan Heroico[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
✅ 🎮 Jugabilidad de Acción/Aventura súper pulida: saltos, combate y exploración que se sienten precisos.  
✅ 🗺️ Progresión tipo metroidvania: volver a zonas con nuevas habilidades es adicción legal.  
✅ 🏆 32 logros de Steam: perfecto para los cazadores de dopamina digital.  
✅ ☁️ Steam Cloud: puedes continuar tu sufrimiento/exploración donde sea.  
✅ 🃏 Cromos de Steam: porque claro, también hay que farmear cartitas como adulto funcional.

Lo No Tan Bueno:
❌ 🎮 Compatibilidad parcial con mando: o sea, “sí, pero no me hagas muchas preguntas” 😬  
❌ 🧭 Puede sentirse exigente con la orientación: el juego te dice “explora” y tú traduces “me perdí otra vez” 😵‍💫  
❌ 🧩 Algunos momentos se apoyan mucho en el backtracking: genial si amas explorar; discutible si tu paciencia tiene DLC.  
❌ 👥 Comunidad activa bajita (14 jugadores ahora): no es que esté muerto… digamos que está “durmiendo como héroe legendario” 💤

[h2]Conclusión (Excelente)[/h2]
Monster Boy y el Reino Maldito es de esos juegos que te hacen pensar: “¿por qué no todos los indies de Acción/Aventura vienen así de bien armados?”. Es bonito, se juega delicioso y tiene ese diseño que te premia por ser curioso (y te castiga por creer que “ya revisaste todo”).

Lo controversial: con 14 jugadores actuales, el juego no está “de moda”, pero tampoco lo necesita. Esto no es un battle royale gritando por atención; es una aventura single player que se disfruta en silencio… mientras tú gritas cuando te das cuenta que la salida estaba a la izquierda.

Y con 2367 recomendaciones totales, queda claro que no soy yo el único que cayó en esta trampa encantadora. Si te gustan los metroidvania/plataformeros con exploración y progresión real, vale totalmente la pena.

Monster boy is an excellent game that I had a lot of fun with, and I think it deserves more hype! It has a great ability system where you switch between a diverse set of monster forms, and has clever puzzles that require you to leverage the unique abilities of each form. I think what I enjoyed most of all is that the world is generally upbeat/happy (which is not the norm for this genre) with a really nice set of biomes and great OST. Gameplay is smooth as butter, the art style is cohesive, and the animations are polished.

That said…it has a few flaws. First, one of the areas mid-game has a noticeable difficulty spike, and while I personally still found it fun, I could see how others might find that frustrating. This happens again in the final area. Similarly, the final set of bosses incorporate some puzzles which are not telegraphed super well and require you to repeat the earlier phases of the fights if you can’t figure out the trick. My final complaint is that the economy was not very well balanced toward the endgame, and I would have had to grind for a bit if I wanted to get all the weapons and armor. (The grinding would not have taken long, but it’s still annoying that even if you scavenge the map for all the most powerful pieces of armor you could still end up being gated by cash before you can use it).

Overall, I’d strongly recommend this to any MV fans who don’t mind some challenge on the platforming size of things, and who are willing to put up with a slightly annoying endgame. Caveats aside, I genuinely had a lot of FUN moments in this game, probably more than in Silksong lol.

I tried with my Switch 1 Pro controller and it initially works, but after you open a menu it stops recognizing the controller; somehow the Steam input stops recognizing the controller. It seems the only way to make the controller work is to limit the game to 60 fps or connect the controller via USB. Terrible, the game had an update to run at 120 fps + for what? The problem has been occurring since 2019 and the developers, according to several people, ignore the reports and requests for a fix. Apparently, the Xbox controller works normally in wireless mode, but I only tested it briefly. Terrible, the developers should fix this bizarre error.[b] I don't recommend buying the game; [/b] who knows what other bugs exist in the game/controllers. They have a beautiful game that supports the Switch button prompts and it simply doesn't work with this and other controllers.

I have played a lot of hard metroidvania games, like Blasphemous 1 & 2 and others, but this is by far the most frustrating and punishing. I completed it with a high completion percentage (nearly 90%), but I didn't enjoy it. 
It's not a true metroidvania; it is more like a puzzle platformer with a map and a very bland combat system. The collisions are quite off. Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom is a vibrant and heartfelt revival of a beloved lineage of side-scrolling adventures, crafted by Game Atelier and published by FDG Entertainment. It is both a continuation and reinvention of the Wonder Boy legacy, a series that once defined the blend of platforming, exploration, and RPG elements in the late eighties and early nineties. From the opening scene, the game establishes a tone of whimsy and wonder. You play as Jin, a young hero whose mischievous uncle has unleashed chaos across the land, transforming people and creatures alike through a mysterious curse. What begins as a simple rescue mission soon unfolds into a sprawling journey through beautifully hand-drawn environments, where every transformation and ability reveals new layers of depth and discovery.

The visual design of Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom is immediately striking. Each environment feels alive with color and movement, from lush jungles and underwater temples to molten caverns and icy peaks. The hand-animated art style, filled with expressive characters and intricate details, gives the game the feel of a living cartoon. There’s an attention to artistry that few modern platformers achieve, making every new area a delight to explore. The fluidity of the animation and the richness of the backgrounds make even routine backtracking feel pleasant. Complementing the visuals is a phenomenal soundtrack featuring contributions from several legendary composers such as Yuzo Koshiro, Motoi Sakuraba, and Michiru Yamane. Their combined work results in a musical landscape that constantly shifts between nostalgic melodies and fresh, energetic rhythms, perfectly echoing the game’s balance between tradition and innovation.

At its core, the game is an expertly designed Metroidvania-style adventure built around transformation mechanics. Over the course of the story, Jin gains the ability to transform into various animal forms, each offering unique abilities that fundamentally change how you interact with the world. The pig form can sniff out secrets and detect hidden passages; the snake can crawl through tight spaces and climb walls; the frog can use its tongue to swing from hooks; the lion charges through obstacles and enemies with raw strength; and the dragon can fly and breathe fire. Switching between these forms allows for clever environmental puzzles and a constant sense of progression as new abilities unlock previously unreachable areas. The interconnected design of the world encourages exploration, rewarding curiosity with hidden treasures, upgrades, and shortcuts that make revisiting older zones worthwhile.

The gameplay strikes a careful balance between precision platforming and problem-solving. Each transformation adds a layer of mechanical complexity that keeps the experience fresh. Combat is straightforward but satisfying, with each form offering distinct attacks and advantages suited to particular situations. The pig’s magic projectiles, the lion’s brute strength, and the dragon’s aerial prowess all play a role in making encounters feel dynamic. The puzzles, meanwhile, are thoughtfully crafted to take advantage of the unique properties of each form without feeling contrived. Whether it’s freezing water to create platforms, manipulating switches, or navigating intricate labyrinths, the game continually finds inventive ways to challenge the player’s mastery of its mechanics.

The level of polish in Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom is remarkable, but it is not without a few hurdles. Some players may find the difficulty curve steeper than expected, especially in later sections where precision and quick form-switching are required under pressure. Boss battles, while beautifully animated and mechanically engaging, can be punishing until you learn their attack patterns. There are also moments where the game’s pacing falters slightly, as backtracking through familiar areas can feel repetitive if you are hunting for specific upgrades or secrets. Yet even these moments rarely break the immersion thanks to the sheer quality of the presentation and the satisfaction of mastering the game’s systems.

One of the most rewarding aspects of Monster Boy is its seamless blending of modern game design with nostalgic sensibilities. It feels like a natural evolution of the Wonder Boy formula, refined through years of genre advancement. It respects its roots without becoming trapped by them, offering an experience that feels both timeless and contemporary. The precision of the controls, the generosity of secrets to uncover, and the sense of progression all work together to create an adventure that consistently feels rewarding. Each discovery, whether a hidden chest or a new transformation, delivers a tangible sense of accomplishment that keeps players engaged until the very end.

Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom ultimately succeeds because it understands what makes this genre enduringly appealing. It is a game about growth, exploration, and mastery—a world that invites players to learn its language of transformation and exploration one discovery at a time. Its art, music, and gameplay coalesce into something that feels both classic and revitalized, a rare example of a spiritual successor that surpasses its predecessors in both scope and execution. For fans of Metroidvania adventures, it offers a polished, joyous experience filled with heart and creativity. For newcomers, it stands as a shining example of how traditional 2D platforming can still feel fresh and alive in the modern era.

If platformers aren't your thing, I DON'T recommend this, as there are a lot of tricky moments, and the location design can fluctuate between neat and annoying, (but thank goodness there are no "Meat Boy" sections). Nothing is impossible, but it certainly won't be a walk in the park. There are plenty of secrets, and a wide range of skills are used constantly. Good bosses, plenty of tense moments (they're unlikely to make you want to replay). For those familiar with the series, there are quite a few nice references. And of course, everything looks great and sounds excellent (Yuzo Koshiro is a genius). The time it takes to complete can literally depend on your agility and puzzle-solving speed (don't AFK farm, it's not needed here). Excellent work with the genre and a truly unique creation.

Rejugado y Confirmo : Es el mejor plataformero 2D de la historia del videojuego.

Uno de los principales aspectos que más me encantó de este videojuego fue su apartado artístico. Básicamente, desde que lo probé por primera vez en PlayStation 4, quedé maravillado con lo bonito que se ve. Es un Metroidvania con un excelente diseño de niveles, una historia entretenida, los enemigos son carismáticos, tiene una banda sonora muy agradable y las peleas contra los jefes son en general desafiantes. Algo que posee el título es bastante backtracking, debido a que a lo largo de la aventura obtendremos herramientas y poderes que nos permitirán acceder a zonas ocultas para la obtención de coleccionables y objetos valiosos. Debo señalar que más o menos a partir del 40% del juego aparece un pico de dificultad un poco brusco, pero sigue siendo un juego accesible para los jugadores menos experimentados y también es una obra decente para aquellos jugadores más veteranos y amantes de los Metroidvanias y los plataformeros. Honestamente, me encanta, se los recomiendo a todos.
